reading.body:
The leading multi-agent orchestration frameworks are concentrated in five repositories with over 184,000 combined stars, dominated by Microsoft's AutoGen and CrewAI, both emphasizing agent collaboration and coordination rather than individual model capability.

Multi-agent systems represent a shift from scaling individual models to scaling their coordination. The frameworks here focus on protocols for delegation, communication between agents, and role-based task assignment. This matters for AI infrastructure because orchestration overhead—routing queries between agents, managing state, scheduling execution—creates new computational demands beyond raw model inference. A system routing work across multiple agents incurs latency and memory costs that a single large model might avoid.

The emphasis on "interoperability" and "protocol" in these frameworks suggests the ecosystem is preparing for heterogeneous deployment. The A2A protocol and standards-focused licensing indicate builders expect agents to run across different infrastructure, possibly owned by different entities. This distributes computation but requires reliable communication, which in turn depends on network architecture and power availability at multiple sites rather than one concentrated facility. This decentralization may relax peak power draw at single locations but complicates total energy accounting.

The data covers active open-source frameworks and does not include proprietary agent orchestration systems, closed-source production deployments, or infrastructure benchmarks measuring the actual compute and power cost of multi-agent workloads versus single-model inference. It shows what the community is building, not what it is running at scale.
